title: Week 2: dylpr and Census
text:
This week, we practiced using dplyr to work with and organize data in R. We used basic functions such as filter(), select(), mutate(), arrange(), group_by(), and summarize() to explore datasets.
We also learned how to access American Community Survey (ACS) data in R using tidycensus. We discussed the difference between ACS 1-year and 5-year estimates and how ACS data represent estimates based on survey samples rather than complete population counts.

title: Week 2: dylpr and Census
text:
Key Concepts
filter(): selects rows based on conditions.
select(): selects specific columns.
mutate(): creates or modifies variables.
arrange(): sorts observations.
group_by() and summarize(): group observations and calculate summary statistics.
ACS 1-year estimates: use data collected over one year and are available for larger geographic areas.
ACS 5-year estimates: combine five years of survey responses and provide data for smaller geographic areas.
GEOID: a geographic identifier used to identify Census geographic areas.
Long vs. wide data: long data usually stores observations across multiple rows, while wide data places related variables in separate columns.

title: Week 2: dylpr and Census
text:
Reflection
This week helped me better understand both data organization in R and the structure of Census data. One important thing I learned is that ACS values are estimates from samples rather than exact counts. This means that the margin of error is important when interpreting and comparing ACS data.
I also have a better understanding of why data structure matters. Long format can be useful for organizing and analyzing multiple variables consistently, while wide format makes it easier to compare several variables for the same geographic area in one row.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
The question
Every number the American Community Survey publishes is an estimate drawn from a sample, not a count. That means every number comes with a margin of error — a statement about how wrong it might be.
Most people ignore it. In this assignment, In this assignment, I examine median gross rent across counties and county-equivalents in Virginia. I compare their margins of error to identify which communities are measured more reliably and which have greater uncertainty.

my_variable <- "B25064_001"     # the variable code, in quotes

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: How big is the margin of error?
text:
How big is the margin of error?
A margin of error of 3,000 means something very different for an estimate of 20,000 than for an estimate of 200,000. To compare across places, we need it as a percentage.

county_data <- county_data %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = moe / estimate * 100)

Now sort to see which counties are measured least reliably.

county_data %>%
  arrange(desc(moe_pct)) %>%
  select(NAME, estimate, moe, moe_pct) %>%
  head(10)

# A tibble: 10 × 4
   NAME                            estimate   moe moe_pct
   <chr>                              <dbl> <dbl>   <dbl>
 1 Surry County, Virginia               858   257    30.0
 2 Greene County, Virginia             1502   409    27.2
 3 Covington city, Virginia             822   220    26.8
 4 Powhatan County, Virginia           1107   293    26.5
 5 King William County, Virginia       1246   296    23.8
 6 Bath County, Virginia                825   180    21.8
 7 Northumberland County, Virginia     1053   197    18.7

 9 Madison County, Virginia            1048   189    18.0
10 Rappahannock County, Virginia       1384   241    17.4


Surry County has the largest margin of error relative to its estimate. Its margin of error is approximately 30.0% of the estimated median gross rent, making it the least reliably measured geography in this dataset.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
section: Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
text:
Is the margin of error bigger in small places?
To answer this we need population and our variable side by side, in the same row. This requires a wide-format ACS pull.

county_wide <- get_acs(
  geography = "county",
  variables = c(myvar = my_variable,
                pop   = "B01003_001"),
  state = my_state,
  year = 2023,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)

head(county_wide)

# A tibble: 6 × 6
  GEOID NAME                        myvarE myvarM   popE  popM
  <chr> <chr>                        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 51001 Accomack County, Virginia      973     59  33326    NA
2 51003 Albemarle County, Virginia    1623     38 113683    NA
3 51005 Alleghany County, Virginia     774    109  14962    NA
4 51007 Amelia County, Virginia        972    126  13342    NA
5 51009 Amherst County, Virginia       842     38  31385    NA
6 51011 Appomattox County, Virginia    883     73  16424    NA



county_wide <- county_wide %>%
  mutate(moe_pct = myvarM / myvarE * 100) %>%
  mutate(reliability = case_when(
    moe_pct < 5  ~ "High confidence",
    moe_pct < 15 ~ "Moderate",
    TRUE         ~ "Low confidence"
  ))

Now compare the average population of counties in each reliability category.

county_wide %>%
  group_by(reliability) %>%
  summarize(
    n_counties = n(),
    avg_population = mean(popE, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  reliability     n_counties avg_population
  <chr>                <int>          <dbl>
1 High confidence         49        134521.
2 Low confidence          13         12508.
3 Moderate                71         26808.


High-confidence counties have an average population of approximately 134,521, while low-confidence counties have an average population of only 12,508. Moderate-confidence counties fall in between, with an average population of about 26,808. This shows a clear pattern: counties with smaller populations tend to have larger margins of error relative to their estimates.

title: Assignment 2: Who Do We Know the Least About?
text:
What this means for policy
The ACS data show that we know the least about some smaller communities in Virginia when measuring median gross rent. Surry County has the largest relative margin of error at 30.0%, followed by Greene County at 27.2%, Covington city at 26.8%, and Powhatan County at 26.5%. These large margins of error mean that their rent estimates are less precise than estimates for communities with smaller margins of error.
This pattern is related to how the ACS works. The ACS is based on a sample rather than a complete count of every household. Smaller communities generally have smaller samples, which creates more uncertainty in their estimates. My results show this pattern clearly. High-confidence counties have an average population of about 134,521, while low-confidence counties have an average population of only 12,508. Moderate-confidence counties fall in between, with an average population of about 26,808.
This uncertainty could cause problems if a state agency used median gross rent to allocate affordable housing funding or rental assistance while treating every estimate as equally certain. Smaller communities with large margins of error would be especially vulnerable. For example, if their estimated rent is lower than the actual rent, they might receive less housing assistance than they actually need. If it is higher than the actual rent, funding might be directed there instead of to communities with greater needs. Therefore, agencies should consider both ACS estimates and their margins of error when making funding decisions.

text: This analysis evaluates claims about changes in poverty in Philadelphia using ACS 5-year estimates. The article compares poverty conditions between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS periods. Because the neighborhood boundaries used in the article are not published Census geographies, this analysis evaluates change at the census tract level.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text: This analysis evaluates claims about changes in poverty in Philadelphia using ACS 5-year estimates. The article compares poverty conditions between the 2006–2010 and 2013–2017 ACS periods. Because the neighborhood boundaries used in the article are not published Census geographies, this analysis evaluates change at the census tract level.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 1 — Reconstruct
The analysis uses ACS 5-year estimates for Philadelphia census tracts. I use table B17001, Poverty Status in the Past 12 Months by Sex by Age. Variable B17001_001 represents the total population for whom poverty status is determined, while B17001_002 represents the population whose income in the past 12 months was below the poverty level.
I use the 2010 ACS 5-year estimate to represent 2006–2010 and the 2017 ACS 5-year estimate to represent 2013–2017. These periods do not overlap. Because the article does not publish the exact census tracts used to construct its neighborhood estimates, I analyze individual census tracts rather than attempting to reproduce the article’s neighborhood boundaries.

ACS data


Show code
#download 2010 data
poverty_2010 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    total = "B17001_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2010,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)




Show code
#download 2017 data
poverty_2017 <- get_acs(
  geography = "tract",
  variables = c(
    below_poverty = "B17001_002",
    total = "B17001_001"
  ),
  state = "PA",
  county = "Philadelphia",
  year = 2017,
  survey = "acs5",
  output = "wide"
)




Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  )

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    poverty_rate = below_povertyE / totalE,
    poverty_moe = moe_prop(
      below_povertyE, totalE,
      below_povertyM, totalM
    )
  )

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 2 — Test
For each census tract, I calculate the poverty rate and its margin of error. I then evaluate estimate reliability using the coefficient of variation (CV), compare poverty rates between the two ACS periods, and test whether the observed changes are statistically distinguishable from zero at the 90% confidence level.

Missing values
Seven census tracts in 2006–2010 and eight census tracts in 2013–2017 have a total population of zero for whom poverty status is determined. Because a poverty rate cannot be calculated when the denominator is zero, these tracts are excluded from the rate and change analysis.


Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  filter(totalE > 0)

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  filter(totalE > 0)




Estimate reliability


Show code
poverty_2010 <- poverty_2010 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

poverty_2017 <- poverty_2017 %>%
  mutate(
    cv = (poverty_moe / 1.645) / poverty_rate * 100,
    reliability = case_when(
      cv < 12 ~ "Reliable",
      cv <= 40 ~ "Somewhat reliable",
      TRUE ~ "Unreliable"
    )
  )

2 Somewhat reliable   321
3 Unreliable           45


Show code

# A tibble: 3 × 2

  <chr>             <int>
1 Reliable             22
2 Somewhat reliable   332
3 Unreliable           22




Change over time


Show code
poverty_change <- poverty_2010 %>%
  select(
    GEOID,
    rate_2010 = poverty_rate,
    moe_2010 = poverty_moe
  ) %>%
  inner_join(
    poverty_2017 %>%
      select(
        GEOID,
        NAME,
        rate_2017 = poverty_rate,
        moe_2017 = poverty_moe
      ),
    by = "GEOID"
  )




Show code
poverty_tested <- poverty_change %>%
  mutate(
    change = rate_2017 - rate_2010,
    se_2010 = moe_2010 / 1.645,
    se_2017 = moe_2017 / 1.645,
    se_diff = sqrt(se_2010^2 + se_2017^2),
    moe_diff = se_diff * 1.645,
    z = change / se_diff,
    significant = abs(z) > 1.645
  )




Show code

  mutate(
    rate_2010_pct = rate_2010 * 100,
    rate_2017_pct = rate_2017 * 100,
    change_pct = change * 100,
    moe_diff_pct = moe_diff * 100,
    tract = str_extract(NAME, "Census Tract [^,]+")

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 3 — Adjudicate

Supported
The article’s broader claim that poverty increased substantially in some parts of Philadelphia is supported by the tract-level analysis. Of the 376 census tracts included in the comparison, 63 experienced a statistically detectable change in poverty rate at the 90% confidence level. Among these, 36 tracts experienced a significant increase and 27 experienced a significant decrease. This confirms that meaningful increases in poverty occurred in some parts of the city, although they were not universal.


Not supported
The data do not support treating most apparent changes across Philadelphia as clear evidence of real change. Of the 376 tracts analyzed, 313 did not show a statistically detectable change. In addition, most poverty-rate estimates were classified as only “Somewhat reliable.” Therefore, differences between the two ACS periods should not automatically be interpreted as meaningful change without considering margins of error.


Cannot be determined
Several of the article’s most specific claims cannot be reproduced with this analysis. The article reports that Eastwick had the largest poverty-rate increase, that Holmesburg’s poverty rate rose from 2% to 19%, and that Fairhill had a 61% poverty rate. However, the article does not publish the census tracts used to construct its neighborhood boundaries, so these neighborhood-level estimates cannot be directly replicated using tract-level data.
The claim that poverty increased specifically among white residents also cannot be evaluated with this analysis because the variables used here measure overall poverty rather than poverty by race. Claims about changes in neighborhood income inequality also require additional income variables that are not included in this analysis.

title: Verify the Claim: Poverty Change in Philadelphia
text:
Part 4 — Rewrite
Philadelphia’s 2013–2017 ACS estimates suggest that poverty increased in some parts of the city, but the pattern is less uniform than raw neighborhood comparisons imply. Among 376 census tracts analyzed, 63 showed a statistically detectable change in poverty rate compared with 2006–2010: 36 increased and 27 decreased. The remaining 313 tracts did not show a change that could be distinguished from sampling uncertainty at the 90% confidence level. Most tract-level estimates were also only somewhat reliable based on their coefficients of variation. Because the original article does not publish the census tracts used to define neighborhoods such as Eastwick, Fairhill, and Holmesburg, its specific neighborhood-level claims cannot be directly reproduced here. The ACS indicates real pockets of worsening poverty, but many apparent changes should be interpreted cautiously.

title: Week 3: Data Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text:
Key Concepts
Anscombe’s Quartet: four datasets can have similar means, correlations, and regression lines but look very different when visualized.
ggplot(data): creates the basic plotting canvas using a dataset.
aes(): defines aesthetic mappings between variables and visual properties such as the x-axis and y-axis.
geom_point(): creates a scatterplot and is useful for examining relationships between two variables.
geom_histogram(): shows how the values of one variable are distributed.
geom_boxplot(): compares the distribution of a variable across groups.
geom_col(): creates a bar chart using values already contained in the data.
geom_line(): shows how a variable changes over time.
geom_errorbar(): displays uncertainty around an estimate using upper and lower bounds such as estimate - moe and estimate + moe.
Coefficient of variation (CV): a relative measure of sampling error calculated as standard error divided by the estimate and multiplied by 100.
Standard error (SE): for ACS estimates, it can be calculated from the 90% margin of error using SE = MOE / 1.645.
Derived uncertainty: margins of error cannot simply be added when estimates are combined.
moe_sum(): calculates uncertainty when adding estimates together.
moe_prop(): calculates uncertainty when one estimate is expressed as a proportion of another and the numerator is a subset of the denominator.
moe_ratio(): calculates uncertainty for a ratio when the numerator is not a subset of the denominator.
Change over time: when comparing estimates from two ACS periods, the uncertainty from both estimates must be considered. The standard error of the difference can be calculated using the standard errors from both periods.

title: Week 3: Data Visualization and ACS Uncertainty
text:
Reflection
This week helped me understand why visualization is important before relying on summary statistics.
I also learned that choosing a visualization depends on the question I want to answer. For example, a histogram is useful for examining a distribution, while a scatterplot is useful for studying the relationship between two variables.
The discussion of uncertainty also helped me better understand ACS data. A visible difference between two estimates does not necessarily mean that a real change occurred. When comparing estimates across time, I need to consider the margins of error and determine whether the uncertainty interval around the change includes zero.

This function runs 10-fold cross-validation with the same seed every time, so every model in your log is tested on the same folds. You don’t need to change it. Read it once so you know what it does.

ctrl <- trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10)

cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {

         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1: don't drop rows).")
  }

  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm", trControl = ctrl)
  fit$results$RMSE
}

Part 3: Getting data from Philadelphia’s open data portal
Many of the city’s datasets on OpenDataPhilly are served through a Carto SQL API. You send a SQL query in a URL, and it sends back data. Ask for format=GeoJSON and st_read() reads the result directly, just like the Indego feed in Week 4.
The pattern:
https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=SELECT ... FROM table_name WHERE ...
Three pieces of SQL are all you need:

SELECT the_geom, column1, column2 chooses which columns come back. Always include the_geom, or you get no geometry.
FROM table_name chooses the dataset.
WHERE ... filters rows. Filter in the query, not in R. Some tables have millions of rows, and pulling everything will be slow or fail.

This helper builds the URL for you. Spaces and symbols in a URL need encoding, and URLencode() handles that.


Code
carto_get <- function(sql) {
  url <- paste0("https://phl.carto.com/api/v2/sql?format=GeoJSON&q=", URLencode(sql))
  st_read(url, quiet = TRUE)
}

Part 5: Transforming features
Watch the October 9 recorded lecture before you start this part. Below is a summary to work from.
So far, every predictor has entered the model as a straight line: each additional unit of X changes predicted Y by the same amount, everywhere. Transformations let the model bend. For prediction, the question is simply does the bend lower CV RMSE? For interpretation, each transformation changes what a coefficient means, so you need to know how to read it.






TipTransform predictors, not your outcome



Keep your outcome y untransformed in this assignment. If you model log(y), your CV RMSE comes out in log units and can’t be compared to the other rows in your log. (Predicting a logged outcome well requires back-transforming, which is an A4 topic.)



5A: Logs, for skewed predictors
Many urban variables are skewed: a few tracts have huge values, and most have small ones. Income, density, and counts are typical. A log compresses the long tail, so a model can use the difference between 1 and 10 as well as the difference between 100 and 1,000.


Code
ggplot(tracts, aes(x = burglary_per_sqmi)) + geom_histogram(bins = 30) + theme_minimal()









Code

Warninglog(0) doesn’t exist



log(0) is -Inf, and it will break your model. Counts and densities often include zeros. Use log1p(x), which computes log(x + 1), for anything that can be 0.


Reading the coefficient: when a predictor is logged, a 1% increase in X goes with a change of about β/100 in Y, in Y’s units. With log1p, this reading is approximate for small values of X.


5B: Squared terms, for curves
If your scatterplot bends (rising and then flattening, or falling and then rising), a squared term lets the line curve. Write it with I(), which tells R to do the arithmetic rather than read ^ as formula syntax.

m_sq <- lm(y ~ dist_ch_mi + I(dist_ch_mi^2), data = tracts)

Sometimes a number works better as groups, either because the relationship isn’t smooth or because the categories are meaningful. You can make categories from any variable with case_when() or cut(), and then make sure R treats them as a factor.

tracts <- tracts %>%
  mutate(
    ring = case_when(

Part 7: Reflection (about 300 words)
Answer in prose, drawing on your model log (incorporate our words of the day for bonus points. just kidding):

What helped, and what didn’t? Name the feature that lowered CV RMSE the most and the one that disappointed you most. Offer a reason for each.
Read one coefficient twice. Choose a variable in your final model. Give its β̂ reading and its ŷ reading in one sentence each.

How much of the remaining error might be uncertainty or statistical noise? Use your last plot.

Your answer: ### Reflection
This assignment showed that spatial features can improve predictions of household vehicle availability beyond traditional ACS socioeconomic variables. The baseline model had a cross-validated RMSE of 11.94 percentage points, which decreased to 9.47 in the final model, representing an improvement of approximately 20.7%. Among the individual spatial features tested, street light outage density provided the largest incremental improvement, reducing CV RMSE from 11.15 to 10.52. In contrast, raw street light outage counts contributed very little additional predictive value. This suggests that normalizing spatial events by area may capture neighborhood differences more effectively than raw counts. The addition of distance to City Hall and its squared term further improved prediction, highlighting the importance of geographic location.
One coefficient in the final model is renter percentage (β̂ = 0.1828). In coefficient terms, holding the other predictors constant, a one-percentage-point increase in renter households is associated with a 0.183-percentage-point increase in the predicted share of households without vehicles. In prediction terms, two otherwise identical tracts with renter percentages of 40% and 50% would have predicted no-vehicle household shares differing by approximately 1.83 percentage points.
The final residual map shows smaller prediction errors than the baseline, but some clusters remain in central and southern Philadelphia. The model may still be missing factors such as public transit accessibility, parking availability, and walkability. Historical SEPTA transit stop and service data could provide additional spatial predictors.
Finally, the relationship between ACS uncertainty and prediction error is not straightforward. Large residuals occur even in tracts with relatively low coefficients of variation, while the high-CV observations are relatively sparse. Therefore, some remaining error may reflect ACS sampling uncertainty, but omitted neighborhood characteristics, model limitations, and statistical noise also likely contribute.

library(tidyverse)

Code
check_na <- function(formula, df) {
  vars <- all.vars(formula)
  bad <- vars[sapply(vars, function(v) any(is.na(df[[v]])))]
  if (length(bad) > 0) {
    stop("These variables have NAs: ", paste(bad, collapse = ", "),
         ". Fill them or choose another variable (Rule 1).")
  }
}

# 10-fold CV RMSE, same folds every time
cv_rmse <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10))
  fit$results$RMSE
}

# Each house's prediction from the fold where it was held out
cv_pred <- function(formula, data) {
  df <- if (inherits(data, "sf")) st_drop_geometry(data) else data
  check_na(formula, df)
  set.seed(5080)
  fit <- train(formula, data = df, method = "lm",
               trControl = trainControl(method = "cv", number = 10,
                                        savePredictions = "final"))
  fit$pred %>% arrange(rowIndex) %>% pull(pred)
}

# Chicago Data Portal (Socrata) -> sf. `where` is a SoQL filter.
socrata_get <- function(dataset, where, select = NULL, limit = 200000) {
  where <- str_squish(where)

  if (!is.null(select)) q <- paste0(q, "&$select=", URLencode(str_squish(select), reserved = TRUE))

Part 1: Clean and explore
Decide which training sales are market sales. Record each rule, why, and how many it removed. Then explore: at least four plots, including a map of price.
In building our model, we only included homes price/sqft below the 0.1st percentile ($11.70/sqft). Extreme values below this cutoff point appeared to be off-market sales; a lot of larger homes sold for less than expected under ~ $15/sqft, which suggested they weren’t representative/good training observations. We removed 24 training observations due to this reason. On the other end of the spectrum, we removed homes where Price/sqft was above the 99.9th percentile ($1300/sqft). Extreme values above this cutoff point were mostly multi-parcel sales which seemed to reflect the price of the full sale vs. the individual home (e.g., $21.8 million on a 2000 square foot house). This removed 24 training observations.
Lastly, one sale had no census tract match because it was located outside of ACS tract boundaries and had no associated ACS values. Because of this, we removed 1 training observation.
In total, we removed 49 observations. We used price/sqft to try to normalize the metric across home sizes/types. A lot of very expensive (high price/sqft) homes at the high end seemed to be actual sales, possibly more historic homes in more expensive parts of the city.

Our exploration showed that sale prices depend on property characteristics and location. We included relationships between sale price and building size, age, and lot size. Part 2: Build the model
Start with a structure-only baseline. Then add features in steps you can learn from, logging each one. Keep the log in a tibble with columns model, added, cv_rmse, moran_i, notes.


Code
# -----------------------------------------------------------------------
# helper
model_log <- tibble(
  model   = character(),
  added   = character(),
  cv_rmse = numeric(),
  moran_i = numeric(),
  notes   = character()
  )

add_entry <- function(formula, data, name, add, note){
  model_log %>%
    add_row(model = name,
            added = add,
            cv_rmse = cv_rmse(formula, data),
            moran_i = round(cv_moran(formula, data), 4),
            notes = note)
}


plot_resid <- function(formula, model){
  temp <- train %>% select(sale_price, geometry) # temp df w/ price + geom
  temp$pred  <- cv_pred(formula, train) # get predictions
  temp$resid <- temp$sale_price - temp$pred # calc residuals
  
  # plot
  ggplot(temp) +
    geom_sf(aes(color = resid), size = 0.4, alpha = 0.6) +
    scale_color_gradient2(low = "#2166ac", mid = "grey90", high = "#b2182b",
                          midpoint = 0, 
                          limits = c(-300000, 300000), 
                          oob = scales::squish) +
    theme_void() +
    labs(color = "Residual ($)", 
         title = paste("Where model", model, "is wrong"),
         subtitle = "Red = underpredicted, blue = overpredicted")
}

What helped most, and what disappointed you? Use your log.
The most helpful improvements came from ACS socioeconomic variables, neighborhood fixed effects, and interaction between building size and neighborhood.
Adding ACS variables reduced RMSE by $47,385, neighborhood fixed effects reduced it by $24,827 and lowered Moran’s I from 0.3523 to 0.2149. The interaction between building area and neighborhood also made a big difference by reducing RMSE by $19,732.
Some features were less helpful than expected. Nearest CTA stations only improved RMSE by $50, and the distance to nearest school and the percentage of households without vehicles had almost no effect. Distance to Lake Michigan slightly improved RMSE and Moran’s I.
Our residual maps show a clear improvement from the baseline to the final model. The baseline has noticeable spatial clustering of under-predictions in parts of northern Chicago and over-predictions in southern Chicago. These patterns show less in the final model.
Overall, our final model M15 achieved the lowest CV RMSE of $180,925, compared to the $291,320 from baseline. It shows a 37.9% reduction and Moran’s I also decreased from 0.3983 to 0.1667.

Part 4: Where it fails, and who pays
Where does your final model fail worst? Is it guessing too high or too low there, and why do you think so?
Based on the plots above, the model fails the most in the southern part of Chicago, specifically Roseland and South Shore. There are not uniform patterns of guessing too high or too low, rather there is a mix of patterns of overprediction and underprediction. This could be attributed to the fact that there are variables that move in conflicting directions within this region. For example, while the southern part of Chicago may have lower income rates and higher vacancy rates compared to the rest of the city, it is also closer to the lake, the loop, schools, and may have higher amounts of college-educated individuals due to proximity to universities. Thus, because of these conflicting indicators of home price coexisting in one area it may lead to more extreme over- or under-predictions that cannot be uniformly accounted for.
Assessors judge their work with the ratio of predicted value to sale price. A ratio above 1 means the home is over-valued and its owner over-taxed. Does your model’s ratio differ by neighborhood income? Connect your answer to your Part 1 cleaning rules and to “The Tax Divide.”
Based on the ratio of predicted values to sale prices, it seems that homes in the south part of Chicago are over-valued and their owners are over-taxed in comparison to other areas, possibly in part due to the reasons described above. In the initial cleaning stages of our model creation we removed homes that were above the 99.9th percentile in sales price and homes that were below the 0.1th percentile in sales price. This translates to homes that are relatively higher in sales price being under-predicted and homes that are relatively lower in sales prices being over-predicted due to the constrained range of training data. Furthermore, this connects to “The Tax Divide” which exposed how many lower-income households’ homes in Chicago were over-assessed relative to commercial and high-end residential properties. Comparing the two maps that show the ratio of predicted values to sale prices and median income, the model mirrors the same systematic biases present in Cook County’s property tax assessments in which housing in lower-income areas is over-predicted.

Part 6: Reflection (about 300 words, as a team)
Read one coefficient twice: once as β̂, once for what it does to ŷ.
Looking at the coefficient building_000sf β̂ represents the estimated change in sale price associated with a one-unit increase in building size. This is of course assuming that other predictors are held constant. Since building_000sf measures size in thousands of square feet, one unit represents an additional 1,000 square feet. Ŷ is the predicted sale price and so increasing building size by 1,000 square feet changes the prediction according to the coefficient. Since the final model includes a squared building-size term as well as an interaction between square footage and neighborhood, the actual effect β̂ has on ŷ, depends on the properties size and neighborhood.
Would you hand this model to the Assessor? What would you warn them about?
We would not hand this model to the Assessor currently, with the high level of uncertainty in its prediction. The characteristics and variables added to our model helped predict sales price as much as possible while using open data. However, it’s crucial to recognize the major limitations inherent in our model. This model is trained on properties sold between 2023 and 2025, which does not represent all properties. Since we used median inputs for some missing property characteristics there is a chance these characteristics are skewed from the reality of the situation. We applied specific criteria to remove outliers. Therefore, the model is not trained on the complete dataset and therefore might be less accurate in predicting extremely high and low priced houses. It’s also important to note that just because a low RMSE score is achievable does not mean that prediction errors across neighborhoods and income groups don’t exist. The model and data used to feed the model could systematically under or overvalue homes in particular neighborhoods. Most importantly, our final model m15’s CV RMSE of $180,925 indicates a substantial prediction error. An error of this size could result in homeowners paying much more or less in taxes than they should. This level of uncertainty is still extraordinarily significant to be used as a prediction model. The final model would need to be significantly altered to even be considered being sent over to an Assessor.
